content: Microsoft Excel, officially known as Microsoft Office Excel, is a spreadsheet software developed and distributed by Microsoft for use on Microsoft Windows and Mac OS X platforms. It provides users with tools for performing calculations, creating graphs, utilizing pivot tables, and programming macros through a language called Visual Basic for Applications (VBA). Notably, Excel 2008 for Mac OS X does not include VBA support. Since its version 5 release in 1993, Excel has been the dominant spreadsheet application for these platforms and is bundled as part of the Microsoft Office suite. It remains one of the most widely used microcomputer applications to date. Historical Development Microsoft initially introduced a spreadsheet program called Multiplan in 1982, which gained popularity on CP/M systems. However, it lost traction on MS-DOS systems to Lotus 1-2-3. The first version of Excel was launched for the Macintosh in 1985, followed by the first Windows version (Excel 2.05) in November 1987. This Windows version was bundled with a runtime Windows environment. By 1988, Excel began outselling Lotus 1-2-3, as Lotus was slow to adapt its software for Windows. This success helped Microsoft establish itself as a leading PC software developer and a strong competitor in the software industry. Microsoft continued to release new versions of Excel approximately every two years, further solidifying its dominance. The current version for Windows is Excel 12, also known as Microsoft Office Excel 2007, while the latest version for Mac OS X is Microsoft Excel 2008. Early in its history, Excel faced a trademark lawsuit from a company that had already been selling a financial software package named Excel. As a result, Microsoft was required to refer to its product as Microsoft Excel in official documents. Over time, this issue was resolved when Microsoft acquired the trademark rights. The program's icon still features a stylized XL, and its default file extension is .xls. Excel introduced several innovations to spreadsheet software. It was the first to allow users to customize the appearance of spreadsheets, including fonts, character attributes, and cell formatting. It also implemented intelligent cell recomputation, updating only dependent cells when a change is made, unlike earlier programs that recalculated all cells or required manual updates. Excel offers robust graphing capabilities and supports mail merge functionality. When Microsoft Office was introduced in 1993, Excel's graphical user interface (GUI) influenced the redesign of Microsoft Word and PowerPoint for consistency. Since 1993, Excel has included VBA, a programming language based on Visual Basic, which enables task automation and the creation of user-defined functions (UDFs). VBA includes a fully integrated development environment (IDE) and supports macro recording to replicate user actions. It also allows the creation of forms and in-worksheet controls for user interaction. Later versions of VBA introduced support for class modules, enabling basic object-oriented programming techniques. However, the automation capabilities of VBA made Excel a target for macro viruses, which became a significant issue in corporate environments. Microsoft addressed this by introducing options to disable macros, enable them selectively, or trust macros signed with a trusted certificate. Versions Excel has been released in various versions for different platforms: Windows Versions: 1987: Excel 2.0 1990: Excel 3.0 1992: Excel 4.0 1993: Excel 5.0 (Office 4.2 & 4.3, with a 32-bit version for Windows NT on PowerPC, DEC Alpha, and MIPS) 1995: Excel for Windows 95 (version 7.0, included in Office 95) 1997: Excel 97 (included in Office 97, with x86 and DEC Alpha versions) 1999: Excel 2000 (version 9.0, included in Office 2000) 2001: Excel 2002 (version 10, included in Office XP) 2003: Excel 2003 (version 11, included in Office 2003) 2007: Excel 2007 (version 12, included in Office 2007) Macintosh Versions: 1985: Excel 1.0 1988: Excel 1.5 1989: Excel 2.2 1990: Excel 3.0 1992: Excel 4.0 1993: Excel 5.0 (Office 4.x, including Motorola 68000 and PowerPC versions) 1998: Excel 8.0 (Office 98) 2000: Excel 9.0 (Office 2001) 2001: Excel 10.0 (Office v.X) 2004: Excel 11.0 (Office 2004 for Mac) 2008: Excel 12.0 (Office 2008 for Mac) OS/2 Versions: 1989: Excel 2.2 1990: Excel 2.3 1991: Excel 3.0 Earlier versions of Excel were limited in the number of rows and columns they could handle. Versions up to 7.0 supported up to 16,384 rows and 256 columns. Versions 8.0 through 11.0 increased this to 65,536 rows and 256 columns. Version 12.0 expanded the capacity to 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns. File Formats Until Excel 2007, the software primarily used a proprietary binary file format called Binary Interchange File Format (BIFF). Excel 2007 introduced Office Open XML (OOXML) as its primary file format, which is XML-based. While the new format does not support VBA macros, Excel 2007 remains backward compatible with traditional binary formats. Excel can also read legacy formats such as CSV, DBF, SYLK, and DIF. Binary Format The binary format specification was initially available upon request but has been freely downloadable since February 2008 under the Open Specification Promise patent licensing. Office Open XML Excel 2007 and other Microsoft Office 2007 products introduced new file formats as part of the OOXML specification. Programming Excel's VBA programming capabilities allow users to write code in a separate editor, enabling advanced manipulation of spreadsheet data. VBA uses objects to control spreadsheet entries, and the results of the code can be displayed directly in the spreadsheet or on charts. This functionality transforms the spreadsheet into an interactive interface for the code. Criticisms Excel has faced criticism for issues related to accuracy, date handling, and specific display errors in Excel 2007. Accuracy Excel's reliance on floating-point calculations has led to criticism regarding statistical accuracy and the absence of certain statistical tools. Proponents argue that these issues are edge cases affecting a small subset of users who are typically aware of workarounds. Date Problems Excel incorrectly assumes that 1900 is a leap year, a bug inherited from Lotus 1-2-3 for backward compatibility. This issue persists in the Office Open XML file format. Excel also supports an alternative date system based on the 1904 epoch. Excel 2007 Display Error In September 2007, a display error in Excel 2007 was reported. For certain pairs of numbers with a product of 65,535, Excel displayed the result as 100,000. This issue affected approximately 14.5% of such pairs. While the actual stored value was correct, the displayed value was incorrect. Microsoft identified the issue as a flaw in the display logic and released a fix on October 9, 2007. The problem was also resolved in Service Pack 1.
